claim: Basement membranes are complex macromolecular networks underlying all continuous layers of cells.
source: Basement membranes (BMs) are complex macromolecular networks underlying all continuous layers of cells.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Essential components of basement membranes include collagen IV and laminins.
source: Essential components include collagen IV and laminins, which are affected by human genetic variants leading to a range of debilitating conditions including kidney, muscle, and cerebrovascular phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BM composition.

claim: Human genetic variants in collagen IV and laminins lead to debilitating conditions including kidney, muscle, and cerebrovascular phenotypes.
source: Essential components include collagen IV and laminins, which are affected by human genetic variants leading to a range of debilitating conditions including kidney, muscle, and cerebrovascular phenotypes.
evidence: This statement references established clinical knowledge about genetic diseases.

claim: The study resolved the global basement membrane composition of kidney organoids.
source: We resolved their global BM composition and discovered a conserved temporal sequence in BM assembly that paralleled mammalian fetal kidneys.
evidence: This claim is supported by the proteomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Kidney organoids exhibit a conserved temporal sequence in basement membrane assembly that parallels mammalian fetal kidneys.
source: We resolved their global BM composition and discovered a conserved temporal sequence in BM assembly that paralleled mammalian fetal kidneys.
evidence: This is supported by comparative proteomic and immunofluorescence data between organoids and fetal kidneys.

claim: Key basement membrane isoforms emerge during kidney organoid differentiation.
source: We identified the emergence of key BM isoforms, which were altered by a pathogenic variant in COL4A5.
evidence: This is demonstrated through proteomic and immunofluorescence analyses showing temporal expression patterns.

claim: A pathogenic variant in COL4A5 alters basement membrane isoforms in kidney organoids.
source: We identified the emergence of key BM isoforms, which were altered by a pathogenic variant in COL4A5.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Alport syndrome patient-derived organoids.

claim: Basement membrane composition is dynamically regulated through development to adulthood.
source: Integrating organoid, fetal, and adult kidney proteomes, we found dynamic regulation of BM composition through development to adulthood, and with single-cell transcriptomic analysis we mapped the cellular origins of BM components.
evidence: This is supported by comparative proteomic analysis across developmental stages.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis mapped the cellular origins of basement membrane components.
source: Integrating organoid, fetal, and adult kidney proteomes, we found dynamic regulation of BM composition through development to adulthood, and with single-cell transcriptomic analysis we mapped the cellular origins of BM components.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of published scRNA-seq datasets.

claim: Basement membranes are composed of laminins, collagen IV, nidogens, and heparan-sulfate proteoglycans.
source: They are composed of laminins, collagen IV, nidogens, heparan-sulfate proteoglycans (Kruegel and Miosge, 2010), and many minor components that combine to form biochemically distinct BMs across different tissues (Randles et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Basement membranes combine to form biochemically distinct structures across different tissues.
source: They are composed of laminins, collagen IV, nidogens, heparan-sulfate proteoglycans (Kruegel and Miosge, 2010), and many minor components that combine to form biochemically distinct BMs across different tissues (Randles et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Basement membranes play active morphogenic roles critical for tissue and cell fate specification.
source: BMs play active morphogenic roles that are critical for tissue and cell fate specification (Kyprianou et al., 2020; Li et al., 2003), and variants in BM genes are associated with a broad range of human diseases (Chew and Lennon, 2018; Gatseva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Variants in basement membrane genes are associated with a broad range of human diseases.
source: BMs play active morphogenic roles that are critical for tissue and cell fate specification (Kyprianou et al., 2020; Li et al., 2003), and variants in BM genes are associated with a broad range of human diseases (Chew and Lennon, 2018; Gatseva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Basement membranes form early in embryogenesis through binding interactions with cell surface receptors.
source: BMs form early in embryogenesis through binding interactions with cell surface receptors (Miner and Yurchenco, 2004) and typically an initial laminin network is required for further incorporation of collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan into nascent BMs (Jayadev et al., 2019; Matsubayashi et al., 2017), thus following an assembly hierarchy for de novo BM formation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: An initial laminin network is required for further incorporation of collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan into nascent basement membranes.
source: BMs form early in embryogenesis through binding interactions with cell surface receptors (Miner and Yurchenco, 2004) and typically an initial laminin network is required for further incorporation of collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan into nascent BMs (Jayadev et al., 2019; Matsubayashi et al., 2017), thus following an assembly hierarchy for de novo BM formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Basement membranes follow an assembly hierarchy for de novo formation.
source: BMs form early in embryogenesis through binding interactions with cell surface receptors (Miner and Yurchenco, 2004) and typically an initial laminin network is required for further incorporation of collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan into nascent BMs (Jayadev et al., 2019; Matsubayashi et al., 2017), thus following an assembly hierarchy for de novo BM formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge.

claim: Basement membranes are highly dynamic and remodel during morphogenesis to form tissue-specific structures.
source: BMs are also highly dynamic, remodeling during morphogenesis to form tissue-specific BMs (Bonnans et al., 2014), such as the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) in the kidney, which functions as a size-selective filter.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The glomerular basement membrane functions as a size-selective filter.
source: BMs are also highly dynamic, remodeling during morphogenesis to form tissue-specific BMs (Bonnans et al., 2014), such as the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) in the kidney, which functions as a size-selective filter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM function.

claim: The glomerular basement membrane is situated between podocytes and endothelial cells in the glomerular capillary wall.
source: Situated between podocytes and endothelial cells in the glomerular capillary wall, the GBM is formed by the fusion of separate podocyte and endothelial BMs, and further remodeled into a mature GBM.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The glomerular basement membrane is formed by the fusion of separate podocyte and endothelial basement membranes.
source: Situated between podocytes and endothelial cells in the glomerular capillary wall, the GBM is formed by the fusion of separate podocyte and endothelial BMs, and further remodeled into a mature GBM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM development.

claim: Glomerular basement membrane maturation involves replacement of laminin-111 and collagen IV α1α1α2 networks by laminin-511 then -521, and collagen IV α3α4α5.
source: This involves replacement of laminin α1β1γ1 (termed laminin-111) and collagen IV α1α1α2 networks by laminin-511 then -521, and collagen IV α3α4α5 (Abrahamson et al., 2013; Abrahamson and St John, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Isoform transitions are important for long-term glomerular basement membrane function.
source: These transitions are important for long-term GBM function, and genetic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 or the laminin gene LAMB2 cause defective GBMs and human diseases (Barker et al., 1990; Zenker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Genetic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 or LAMB2 cause defective glomerular basement membranes and human diseases.
source: These transitions are important for long-term GBM function, and genetic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 or the laminin gene LAMB2 cause defective GBMs and human diseases (Barker et al., 1990; Zenker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics has enabled global analyses of basement membrane composition.
source: Most understanding about vertebrate BMs comes from immunolocalization and genetic knockout studies (Abrahamson et al., 2013), and for composition, mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics has enabled global analyses (Naba et al., 2016; Randles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous proteomic studies.

claim: Proteomics allows time course studies that provide insight into matrix dynamics during development and disease progression.
source: Proteomics also allows time course studies, which have provided insight into matrix dynamics during development and in disease progression (Hebert et al., 2020; Lipp et al., 2021; Naba et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Proteomics lacks the spatial context that is captured by localization studies.
source: However, proteomics lacks the spatial context that is captured by localization studies, including fluorescent tagging of endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is a known limitation of proteomic approaches.

claim: Investigations in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans have unraveled dynamic features of basement membrane assembly in embryogenesis and repair.
source: Such investigations in Drosophila melanogaster and Caenorhabditis elegans have unraveled dynamic features of BM assembly in embryogenesis and repair (Howard et al., 2019; Keeley et al., 2020; Matsubayashi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in model organisms.

claim: Kidney organoids generated from pluripotent stem cells contain self-organized 3D structures with multiple kidney cell types.
source: Kidney organoids generated from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) contain self-organized 3D structures with multiple kidney cell types and represent an attractive system for investigating early development (Combes et al., 2019b; Takasato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous organoid studies.

claim: Kidney organoids represent an attractive system for investigating early development.
source: Kidney organoids generated from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) contain self-organized 3D structures with multiple kidney cell types and represent an attractive system for investigating early development (Combes et al., 2019b; Takasato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a conclusion from previous work.

claim: Organoids derived from induced pluripotent stem cells have use in personalized disease modeling and therapy screening.
source: Organoids derived from induced PSCs (iPSCs), reprogrammed from patient somatic cells, have further use in personalized disease modeling and therapy screening (Czerniecki et al., 2018; Forbes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During differentiation, kidney organoids pattern into early nephron structures with clusters of podocytes and endothelial cells, and a complex tubular epithelial system.
source: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney, and during differentiation, kidney organoids pattern into early nephron structures with clusters of podocytes and endothelial cells, and a complex tubular epithelial system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about organoid differentiation.

claim: Kidney organoids show transcriptomic homology to the first trimester human fetal kidney.
source: Furthermore, organoids show transcriptomic homology to the first trimester human fetal kidney (Takasato et al., 2015), and differentiation is further advanced by in vivo implantation (Bantounas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Kidney organoid differentiation is further advanced by in vivo implantation.
source: Furthermore, organoids show transcriptomic homology to the first trimester human fetal kidney (Takasato et al., 2015), and differentiation is further advanced by in vivo implantation (Bantounas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Day 18 kidney organoids have glomerular clusters positive for WT1, NPHS1, and CD31.
source: We confirmed differentiation to glomerular clusters (WT1+/NPHS1+/CD31+) and CDH1+ tubular structures in day 18 organoids (Figure 1B) and comparable morphology to mouse and human fetal kidney tissues.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Day 18 kidney organoids have CDH1+ tubular structures.
source: We confirmed differentiation to glomerular clusters (WT1+/NPHS1+/CD31+) and CDH1+ tubular structures in day 18 organoids (Figure 1B) and comparable morphology to mouse and human fetal kidney tissues.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Day 18 kidney organoids have comparable morphology to mouse and human fetal kidney tissues.
source: We confirmed differentiation to glomerular clusters (WT1+/NPHS1+/CD31+) and CDH1+ tubular structures in day 18 organoids (Figure 1B) and comparable morphology to mouse and human fetal kidney tissues.
evidence: This is based on comparative histological analysis.

claim: Day 11 kidney organoids had cell clusters amongst mesenchymal tissue.
source: Day 11 organoids had cell clusters amongst mesenchymal tissue, and at day 14, discernible nephron-like structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Day 14 kidney organoids had discernible nephron-like structures.
source: Day 11 organoids had cell clusters amongst mesenchymal tissue, and at day 14, discernible nephron-like structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Day 18 kidney organoids had regions resembling the nephrogenic zone found at E19 in the mouse and between 8 and 10 weeks post conception in human.
source: At day 18, organoids had regions resembling the nephrogenic zone found at E19 in the mouse and between 8 and 10 weeks post conception (wpc) in human, but lacked distinct corticomedullary differentiation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on comparative histological analysis shown in figures.

claim: Day 18 kidney organoids lacked distinct corticomedullary differentiation.
source: At day 18, organoids had regions resembling the nephrogenic zone found at E19 in the mouse and between 8 and 10 weeks post conception (wpc) in human, but lacked distinct corticomedullary differentiation (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is based on histological observations.

claim: Basement membrane integrin receptors localize adjacent to laminin+ basement membrane-like structures at day 25 of organoid differentiation.
source: By immunofluorescence, we verified the localization of BM integrin receptors adjacent to laminin+ BM-like structures at day 25 of organoid differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Day 25 kidney organoids show advanced podocyte differentiation with primary podocyte processes.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy and immunoelectron microscopy, we observed advanced podocyte differentiation with primary podocyte processes and confirmed assembly of laminin+ BM structures (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 1D and supplements.

claim: Day 25 kidney organoids have laminin+ basement membrane structures confirmed by immunoelectron microscopy.
source: Using transmission electron microscopy and immunoelectron microscopy, we observed advanced podocyte differentiation with primary podocyte processes and confirmed assembly of laminin+ BM structures (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: Likely endothelial cells are present in glomerular structures of day 25 kidney organoids.
source: We also detected likely endothelial cells present in glomerular structures (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and a BM-like matrix between podocytes and endothelial cells in day 25 organoid glomeruli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy observations shown in figures.

claim: A basement membrane-like matrix exists between podocytes and endothelial cells in day 25 organoid glomeruli.
source: We also detected likely endothelial cells present in glomerular structures (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and a BM-like matrix between podocytes and endothelial cells in day 25 organoid glomeruli (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy images.

claim: Kidney organoids mimic the normal progression of kidney differentiation with concomitant assembly of basement membrane structures in vitro.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that kidney organoids mimic the normal progression of kidney differentiation with the concomitant assembly of BM structures in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: The study investigated iPSC lines from patients with Alport syndrome carrying a likely pathogenic X-linked missense variant in COL4A5 (c.3695G>A; p.Gly1232Asp).
source: We selected iPSC lines from a mother and her son, both carrying a likely pathogenic X-linked missense variant in COL4A5 (c.3695G>A; p.Gly1232Asp) and a variant of unknown significance in COL4A4 (c.3286C>T; p.Pro1096Ser; Figure 1E; see Supplementary file 1 and Materials and methods 'Clinical presentation' for further details).
evidence: This is based on genetic testing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The Alport syndrome patients studied also carried a variant of unknown significance in COL4A4 (c.3286C>T; p.Pro1096Ser).
source: We selected iPSC lines from a mother and her son, both carrying a likely pathogenic X-linked missense variant in COL4A5 (c.3695G>A; p.Gly1232Asp) and a variant of unknown significance in COL4A4 (c.3286C>T; p.Pro1096Ser; Figure 1E; see Supplementary file 1 and Materials and methods 'Clinical presentation' for further details).
evidence: This is based on genetic testing data.

claim: Alport syndrome patient-derived organoids progressed through differentiation and formed WT1+/NPHS1+/CDH1+ glomeruli and CDH1+ tubules.
source: AS patient-derived organoids progressed through differentiation and formed WT1+/NPHS1+/CDH1+ glomeruli and CDH1+ tubules (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) with no evident abnormalities by light microscopy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1F.

claim: Alport syndrome organoids had no evident abnormalities by light microscopy.
source: AS patient-derived organoids progressed through differentiation and formed WT1+/NPHS1+/CDH1+ glomeruli and CDH1+ tubules (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) with no evident abnormalities by light microscopy.
evidence: This is based on histological observations.

claim: Alport syndrome and wild-type organoids have comparable distribution of the collagen IV α4 chain.
source: We found comparable distribution of the collagen IV α4 chain in AS and wild-type organoids (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) confirming assembly of a collagen IV α3α4α5 network, which is described in AS patients with missense variants (Yamamura et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Alport syndrome organoids assemble a collagen IV α3α4α5 network.
source: We found comparable distribution of the collagen IV α4 chain in AS and wild-type organoids (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) confirming assembly of a collagen IV α3α4α5 network, which is described in AS patients with missense variants (Yamamura et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data and supported by citation.

claim: Collagen IV α3α4α5 network assembly is described in Alport syndrome patients with missense variants.
source: We found comparable distribution of the collagen IV α4 chain in AS and wild-type organoids (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) confirming assembly of a collagen IV α3α4α5 network, which is described in AS patients with missense variants (Yamamura et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous clinical study.

claim: Laminin compensation is reported in X-linked Alport syndrome.
source: Since laminin compensation is reported in X-linked AS (Abrahamson et al., 2007; Kashtan et al., 2001), we examined the deposition of laminin-β2 (LAMB2) in AS organoids.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Alport syndrome organoids show increased deposition of LAMB2, most notable in extraglomerular basement membranes.
source: We found increased deposition of LAMB2 in AS organoids, most notable in extraglomerular BM (Figure 1G), and further confirmed increased LAMB2 levels by immunoblotting (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence and immunoblotting data in Figures 1G and 1H.

claim: Increased LAMB2 levels in Alport syndrome organoids were confirmed by immunoblotting.
source: We found increased deposition of LAMB2 in AS organoids, most notable in extraglomerular BM (Figure 1G), and further confirmed increased LAMB2 levels by immunoblotting (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblotting data in Figure 1H.

claim: Studies in mouse and invertebrate development have shown a sequence for de novo basement membrane assembly with initial laminin deposition followed by incorporation of collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan.
source: Studies in mouse and invertebrate development have shown a sequence for de novo BM assembly with initial laminin deposition followed by incorporation of collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan (Jayadev et al., 2019; Matsubayashi et al., 2017; Urbano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Day 11 kidney organoids have punctate deposits of pan-laminin in interrupted basement membrane networks around cell clusters.
source: We found punctate deposits of pan-laminin in interrupted BM networks around cell clusters in day 11 organoids, and in continuous BMs surrouding CD31+ endothelial and epithelial structures in day 18 and 25 organoids (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: Day 18 and 25 kidney organoids have continuous basement membranes surrounding CD31+ endothelial and epithelial structures.
source: We found punctate deposits of pan-laminin in interrupted BM networks around cell clusters in day 11 organoids, and in continuous BMs surrouding CD31+ endothelial and epithelial structures in day 18 and 25 organoids (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: COL4A1 was weakly detected in day 11 kidney organoids.
source: Conversely, COL4A1 was weakly detected in day 11 organoids but was partially co-distributed with laminin at day 18, and within continuous BM networks at day 25 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: COL4A1 was partially co-distributed with laminin at day 18 in kidney organoids.
source: Conversely, COL4A1 was weakly detected in day 11 organoids but was partially co-distributed with laminin at day 18, and within continuous BM networks at day 25 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: COL4A1 was within continuous basement membrane networks at day 25 in kidney organoids.
source: Conversely, COL4A1 was weakly detected in day 11 organoids but was partially co-distributed with laminin at day 18, and within continuous BM networks at day 25 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: Nidogen and perlecan colocalized in discrete, interrupted basement membranes in day 11 kidney organoids.
source: Nidogen and perlecan colocalized in discreet, interrupted BMs in day 11 organoids and later in linear BM networks around tubules and NPHS1+ glomerular structures at days 18 and 25 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B.

claim: Nidogen and perlecan colocalized in linear basement membrane networks around tubules and NPHS1+ glomerular structures at days 18 and 25 in kidney organoids.
source: Nidogen and perlecan colocalized in discreet, interrupted BMs in day 11 organoids and later in linear BM networks around tubules and NPHS1+ glomerular structures at days 18 and 25 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B.

claim: Kidney organoids recapitulate the sequence of basement membrane assembly described in vivo.
source: Together, these findings indicate that kidney organoids recapitulate the sequence of BM assembly described in vivo, reinforcing their fidelity as system for investigating BM developmental dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence data.

claim: The study detected 5,245 proteins in the cellular fraction of kidney organoids.
source: Overall, we detected 5,245 proteins in the cellular fraction and 4,703 in the extracellular fraction (Supplementary file 2), and by cross-referencing our data with the human matrisome list (Naba et al., 2016) we identified 228 matrix proteins in kidney organoids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis data.

claim: The study detected 4,703 proteins in the extracellular fraction of kidney organoids.
source: Overall, we detected 5,245 proteins in the cellular fraction and 4,703 in the extracellular fraction (Supplementary file 2), and by cross-referencing our data with the human matrisome list (Naba et al., 2016) we identified 228 matrix proteins in kidney organoids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis data.

claim: The study identified 228 matrix proteins in kidney organoids.
source: Overall, we detected 5,245 proteins in the cellular fraction and 4,703 in the extracellular fraction (Supplementary file 2), and by cross-referencing our data with the human matrisome list (Naba et al., 2016) we identified 228 matrix proteins in kidney organoids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis cross-referenced with the human matrisome list.

claim: There was an increase in abundance of matrix components from day 14 to 25 in kidney organoids.
source: There was an increase in abundance of matrix components from day 14 to 25 (Figure 3B), and 203 of all matrix proteins found in the organoids (~90%) were detectable at all time points (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 203 of all matrix proteins found in kidney organoids (~90%) were detectable at all time points.
source: There was an increase in abundance of matrix components from day 14 to 25 (Figure 3B), and 203 of all matrix proteins found in the organoids (~90%) were detectable at all time points (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The kidney organoid extracellular fraction was enriched for basement membrane proteins compared to the cellular fraction.
source: The organoid extracellular fraction was enriched for BM proteins compared to the cellular fraction (Figure 3D), which was expected as these are large, highly cross-linked proteins, and hence, difficult to solubilize.
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic data in Figure 3D.

claim: Basement membrane proteins are large, highly cross-linked proteins that are difficult to solubilize.
source: The organoid extracellular fraction was enriched for BM proteins compared to the cellular fraction (Figure 3D), which was expected as these are large, highly cross-linked proteins, and hence, difficult to solubilize.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BM protein biochemistry.

claim: There was an increasing trend for basement membrane protein levels from day 14 to 25 in kidney organoids.
source: Furthermore, we observed an increasing trend for BM protein levels through day 14 to 25 (Figure 3D), again indicating BM deposition over time and corroborating our immunofluorescence findings.
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic data in Figure 3D.

claim: The study identified 78 basement membrane proteins in kidney organoids.
source: In total, we identified 78 BM proteins (Figure 3E), including abundant components that are deposited early in kidney morphogenesis (e.g., COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMA1, LAMB1, LAMC1) (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on proteomic analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMA1, LAMB1, and LAMC1 are abundant basement membrane components deposited early in kidney morphogenesis.
source: In total, we identified 78 BM proteins (Figure 3E), including abundant components that are deposited early in kidney morphogenesis (e.g., COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMA1, LAMB1, LAMC1) (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on proteomic data and represents established knowledge.

claim: LAMA5 and LAMB2 only appeared amongst the most abundant basement membrane components at day 25 in kidney organoids.
source: LAMA5 and LAMB2, two key components of the mature GBM, only appeared amongst the most abundant BM components at day 25 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), thus indicating a temporal expression of GBM laminins during organoid differentiation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: LAMA5 and LAMB2 are key components of the mature glomerular basement membrane.
source: LAMA5 and LAMB2, two key components of the mature GBM, only appeared amongst the most abundant BM components at day 25 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), thus indicating a temporal expression of GBM laminins during organoid differentiation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM composition.

claim: There is temporal expression of glomerular basement membrane laminins during kidney organoid differentiation.
source: LAMA5 and LAMB2, two key components of the mature GBM, only appeared amongst the most abundant BM components at day 25 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), thus indicating a temporal expression of GBM laminins during organoid differentiation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomic data showing temporal changes.

claim: LAMB2 had the highest fold change in upregulation from day 18 to day 25 in kidney organoids, followed by LAMA5 and COL4A3.
source: This was confirmed by marked upregulation of mature GBM proteins from day 18 to day 25, with LAMB2 scoring with the highest fold change followed by LAMA5 and COL4A3 (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic data in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: LAMA5 was enriched from day 14 to day 18 in kidney organoids together with other glomerular basement membrane proteins (COL4A3, AGRN) and early basement membrane collagens and laminins (COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMC1, LAMA1).
source: LAMA5 was also enriched from day 14 to day 18 together with other GBM proteins (COL4A3, AGRN) and early BM collagens and laminins (COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMC1, LAMA1) (Figure 3G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic data in Figures 3G, 3H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: During glomerular basement membrane assembly, an initial laminin-111 network is sequentially replaced by laminin-511 then -521.
source: During GBM assembly, an initial laminin-111 (α1αβ1γ1) network is sequentially replaced by laminin-511 then -521 (Abrahamson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Day 14 to day 18 represents a period of intense basement membrane assembly and initial glomerular basement membrane differentiation in kidney organoids.
source: We therefore reasoned that day 14 to day 18 would represent a period of intense BM assembly and initial GBM differentiation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known sequence of GBM assembly.

claim: Proteins upregulated from day 14 to 18 in kidney organoids showed overrepresentation of terms associated with basement membrane assembly and remodeling, including laminin interactions, degradation of extracellular matrix and collagen chain trimerization.
source: In support of this hypothesis, a pathway enrichment analysis of the proteins upregulated from day 14 to 18 revealed an overrepresentation of terms associated with BM assembly and remodeling, including laminin interactions, degradation of ECM and collagen chain trimerization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on pathway enrichment analysis of proteomic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: COL4A1 appeared at day 11 in kidney organoids and later partially colocalized with laminin at day 14 and as continuous basement membrane networks from day 18.
source: As described earlier, COL4A1 appeared at day 11 (Figure 2A) and later partially colocalized with laminin at day 14 and as continuous BM networks from day 18 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figures 2A and 4A.

claim: COL4A3 was scarce at days 14 and 18 in kidney organoids, but clearly colocalized with laminin in glomerular structures at day 25.
source: Conversely, COL4A3 was scarce at days 14 and 18, but clearly colocalized with laminin in glomerular structures at day 25 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A.

claim: LAMA5 was detected from day 18 in kidney organoids and increased in glomerular structures at day 25.
source: We detected LAMA5 from day 18, and this increased in glomerular structures at day 25.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence observations.

claim: LAMB1 was widely distributed from day 14 to day 25 in kidney organoids.
source: LAMB1 was widely distributed from day 14 to day 25, whereas LAMB2, detected from day 18 onwards, was enriched in glomerular structures at day 25.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence observations.

claim: LAMB2 was detected from day 18 onwards in kidney organoids and was enriched in glomerular structures at day 25.

claim: Understanding of basement membrane assembly and regulation is limited by the lack of appropriate systems to track components that are spatiotemporally regulated and undergo turnover.

evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a known limitation in the field.

claim: Human fetal tissue has limited availability and developmental studies are restricted to static time points.
source: Human fetal tissue has limited availability and developmental studies are restricted to static time points, and the technical limitations of imaging in mouse models also difficult the investigation of the dynamic BM environment in vivo.
evidence: This is a known limitation in developmental biology research.

claim: Technical limitations of imaging in mouse models make it difficult to investigate the dynamic basement membrane environment in vivo.
source: Human fetal tissue has limited availability and developmental studies are restricted to static time points, and the technical limitations of imaging in mouse models also difficult the investigation of the dynamic BM environment in vivo.
evidence: This is a known limitation in developmental biology research.

claim: Kidney organoids have morphological and molecular features comparable to fetal kidney tissue that overcome species differences.
source: Despite the developmental limitations with iPSC-derived kidney organoids, including lack of features such as directional cues, vascularization, and cortical-medullary segmentation (Romero-Guevara et al., 2020), this system has morphological and molecular features comparable to fetal kidney tissue that overcome species differences and provides a complex in vitro environment to examine BM assembly (Bantounas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: iPSC-derived kidney organoids lack features such as directional cues, vascularization, and cortical-medullary segmentation.
source: Despite the developmental limitations with iPSC-derived kidney organoids, including lack of features such as directional cues, vascularization, and cortical-medullary segmentation (Romero-Guevara et al., 2020), this system has morphological and molecular features comparable to fetal kidney tissue that overcome species differences and provides a complex in vitro environment to examine BM assembly (Bantounas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents known limitations of organoid systems.

claim: Kidney organoids provide a complex in vitro environment to examine basement membrane assembly.
source: Despite the developmental limitations with iPSC-derived kidney organoids, including lack of features such as directional cues, vascularization, and cortical-medullary segmentation (Romero-Guevara et al., 2020), this system has morphological and molecular features comparable to fetal kidney tissue that overcome species differences and provides a complex in vitro environment to examine BM assembly (Bantounas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation and the experimental data in this study.

claim: Kidney organoids differentiate into glomerular structures containing the cells required for glomerular basement membrane assembly.
source: We demonstrated that kidney organoids differentiate into glomerular structures containing the cells required for GBM assembly, andother single-cell transcriptomic studies have also shown over 20 other distinct cell populations present in kidney organoids (Combes et al., 2019a; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data in this study.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic studies have shown over 20 distinct cell populations present in kidney organoids.
source: We demonstrated that kidney organoids differentiate into glomerular structures containing the cells required for GBM assembly, andother single-cell transcriptomic studies have also shown over 20 other distinct cell populations present in kidney organoids (Combes et al., 2019a; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cross-talk between different cell types is essential for basement membrane assembly and influences its composition.
source: Cross-talk between different cell types is essential for BM assembly and influences its composition (Byron et al., 2014), hence, the multiple cell types in the organoid system enable BM formation and remodeling.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The multiple cell types in the organoid system enable basement membrane formation and remodeling.
source: Cross-talk between different cell types is essential for BM assembly and influences its composition (Byron et al., 2014), hence, the multiple cell types in the organoid system enable BM formation and remodeling.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the known importance of cell-cell interactions and the cellular complexity of organoids.

claim: Organoids form basement membranes early during differentiation.
source: A key finding from this study is that organoids form BMs early during differentiation and, more importantly, recapitulate a sequence of BM assembly events with initial deposition of laminin followed by incorporation of collagen IV, nidogen, and perlecan (Brown et al., 2017; Sasaki et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a key finding based on the experimental data in this study.

claim: Kidney organoids have provided new insights into disease processes.
source: Kidney organoids have also provided new insights into disease processes (Rooney et al., 2021; Tanigawa et al., 2018; Tian and Lennon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Kidney organoids with a pathological missense variant in COL4A5 differentiated and deposited core basement membrane proteins, including a collagen IV α3α4α5 network.
source: We found that kidney organoids with a pathological missense variant in COL4A5 differentiated and deposited core BM proteins, including a collagen IV α3α4α5 network, which is described in missense variant cases.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from Alport organoids.

claim: Collagen IV α3α4α5 network deposition is described in missense variant cases of Alport syndrome.
source: We found that kidney organoids with a pathological missense variant in COL4A5 differentiated and deposited core BM proteins, including a collagen IV α3α4α5 network, which is described in missense variant cases.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge.

claim: In one study, 64 out of 146 patients with X-linked Alport syndrome had the collagen IV α5 chain in the glomerular basement membrane.
source: In one study, 64 out of 146 patients with X-linked AS had the collagen IV α5 chain in the GBM (Yamamura et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous clinical study.

claim: Despite evidence of protein secretion, the glomerular basement membrane fails to maintain function in Alport syndrome patients with missense variants.
source: Despite evidence of protein secretion, the GBM fails to maintain function in these patients.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about Alport syndrome.

claim: Dysregulation of glomerular laminins, including LAMB2, in patients with Alport syndrome and animal models has been reported.
source: Interestingly, we found increased deposition of LAMB2 in extraglomerular BMs in our Alport organoids. Dysregulation of glomerular laminins, including LAMB2, in patients with AS and animal models has been reported (Abrahamson et al., 2007; Kashtan et al., 2001), but the mechanisms for this are unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanisms for dysregulation of glomerular laminins in Alport syndrome are unclear.
source: Interestingly, we found increased deposition of LAMB2 in extraglomerular BMs in our Alport organoids. Dysregulation of glomerular laminins, including LAMB2, in patients with AS and animal models has been reported (Abrahamson et al., 2007; Kashtan et al., 2001), but the mechanisms for this are unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Alport organoids demonstrate the utility of the organoid system to dissect abnormal mechanisms of basement membrane assembly.
source: Our findings in Alport organoids demonstrate the utility of this system to dissect abnormal mechanisms of BM assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Alport organoid experiments.

claim: The study used mass spectrometry-based proteomics to define global basement membrane composition in kidney organoids.
source: To define global BM composition in kidney organoids, we used MS-based proteomics and identified 78 BM proteins dynamically expressed throughout the kidney organoid differentiation time course.
evidence: This is based on the proteomic methodology and data.

claim: Core glomerular basement membrane components including laminin-521 and collagen IV α3α4α5 were detected in kidney organoids.
source: Core GBM components including laminin-521 and collagen IV α3α4α5, which only appear in mature glomeruli, were also detected.
evidence: This is based on proteomic data.

claim: Laminin-521 and collagen IV α3α4α5 only appear in mature glomeruli.
source: Core GBM components including laminin-521 and collagen IV α3α4α5, which only appear in mature glomeruli, were also detected.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM maturation.

claim: Developmental isoform transitions in the glomerular basement membrane involving laminin and collagen IV are described in humans and rodents.
source: Developmental isoform transitions in the GBM involving laminin and collagen IV are described in humans and rodents (Abrahamson and St John, 1993), and in the current understanding, immature glomeruli assemble a primary GBM containing laminin-111 and collagen IV α1α2α1 that is later replaced, respectively, by laminin-521 and collagen IV α3α4α5 in mature glomeruli.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: Immature glomeruli assemble a primary glomerular basement membrane containing laminin-111 and collagen IV α1α2α1 that is later replaced by laminin-521 and collagen IV α3α4α5 in mature glomeruli.
source: Developmental isoform transitions in the GBM involving laminin and collagen IV are described in humans and rodents (Abrahamson and St John, 1993), and in the current understanding, immature glomeruli assemble a primary GBM containing laminin-111 and collagen IV α1α2α1 that is later replaced, respectively, by laminin-521 and collagen IV α3α4α5 in mature glomeruli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GBM development.

claim: There was a temporal and spatial emergence of mature collagen IV and laminin isoforms within glomerular structures in kidney organoids.
source: In keeping with these observations, we found a temporal and spatial emergence of mature collagen IV and laminin isoforms within glomerular structures in kidney organoids, and in a reanalysis of publicly available scRNA-seq data, we confirmed podocyte expression of mature GBM markers.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence and proteomic data.

claim: Podocyte expression of mature glomerular basement membrane markers was confirmed in kidney organoids.
source: In keeping with these observations, we found a temporal and spatial emergence of mature collagen IV and laminin isoforms within glomerular structures in kidney organoids, and in a reanalysis of publicly available scRNA-seq data, we confirmed podocyte expression of mature GBM markers.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of scRNA-seq data.

claim: Kidney organoids can efficiently recapitulate the spatiotemporal emergence of glomerular basement membrane components.
source: These findings demonstrate that kidney organoids can efficiently recapitulate the spatiotemporal emergence of GBM components.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The triggers for glomerular basement membrane isoform switching remain unknown.
source: The triggers for GBM isoform switching remain unknown, but two regulators, LMX1b and EPB41L5, have been implicated in this.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claim: Studies in Lmxb1 knockout mice suggest that podocyte expression of LMX1b is not essential for initial glomerular basement membrane assembly but is linked to Col4a3/Col4a4 expression during glomerulogenesis.
source: Studies in Lmxb1 knockout mice suggest that podocyte expression of this transcription factor is not essential for initial GBM assembly but is linked to Col4a3/Col4a4 expression during glomerulogenesis as demonstrated by reduced collagen IV α3α4α5 network in the GBM in null Lmxb1 newborn mice (Morello et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Podocyte-specific expression of LMX1b/COL4A3/COL4A4 was found in day 25 kidney organoids.
source: We found podocyte-specific expression of LMX1b/COL4A3/COL4A4 in day 25 kidney organoids and, moreover, confirmed deposition of COL4A3/COL4A4 in a GBM pattern within NPHS2+-glomerular structures in these organoids.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Deposition of COL4A3/COL4A4 in a glomerular basement membrane pattern within NPHS2+-glomerular structures was confirmed in day 25 kidney organoids.
source: We found podocyte-specific expression of LMX1b/COL4A3/COL4A4 in day 25 kidney organoids and, moreover, confirmed deposition of COL4A3/COL4A4 in a GBM pattern within NPHS2+-glomerular structures in these organoids.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data.

claim: Podocyte expression of EPB41L5 was linked to glomerular basement membrane assembly in vivo and incorporation of laminin-511/521 into podocyte-derived extracellular basement membrane networks in vitro.
source: In addition, podocyte expression of EPB41L5, a component of the podocyte integrin adhesion complex, was linked to GBM assembly in vivo and incorporation of laminin-511/521 into podocyte-derived extracellular BM networks in vitro (Maier et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: EPB41L5 was detected in kidney organoid and mouse proteomic datasets.
source: In this study, we detected EPB41L5 in kidney organoid and mouse proteomic datasets, with cell expression patterns matching that of LAMA5, indicating the potential for this system to unravel further insights into GBM regulation.
evidence: This is based on proteomic data.

claim: EPB41L5 cell expression patterns matched that of LAMA5 in kidney organoids.
source: In this study, we detected EPB41L5 in kidney organoid and mouse proteomic datasets, with cell expression patterns matching that of LAMA5, indicating the potential for this system to unravel further insights into GBM regulation.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data.

claim: Kidney organoids have potential to unravel further insights into glomerular basement membrane regulation.
source: In this study, we detected EPB41L5 in kidney organoid and mouse proteomic datasets, with cell expression patterns matching that of LAMA5, indicating the potential for this system to unravel further insights into GBM regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the expression data.

claim: One proteomic study of mouse kidney development defined the global extracellular matrix composition through development to adulthood and described a sequence of changes in the interstitial matrix over development.
source: There are a few proteomic studies addressing the spatiotemporal changes in BM during development. One study of mouse kidney development defined the global ECM composition through development to adulthood and described a sequence of changes in the interstitial matrix over development (Lipp et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The study's sample fractionation strategy and analytical pipeline detected a further 130 matrix proteins compared to a previous study, including key glomerular basement membrane components and basement membrane regulators.
source: With our sample fractionation strategy and analytical pipeline, we detected a further 130 matrix proteins, including key GBM components (COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5) and BM regulators such as PAPLN and HMCN1 (Keeley et al., 2020; Morrissey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparative proteomic analysis.

claim: PAPLN and HMCN1 are basement membrane regulators.
source: With our sample fractionation strategy and analytical pipeline, we detected a further 130 matrix proteins, including key GBM components (COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5) and BM regulators such as PAPLN and HMCN1 (Keeley et al., 2020; Morrissey et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Late-stage kidney organoids (at day 25) and mouse kidneys at E19 share a very comparable basement membrane protein profile.
source: Our findings further demonstrated that late-stage kidney organoids (at day 25) and mouse kidneys at E19 share a very comparable BM protein profile.
evidence: This is based on comparative proteomic analysis.

claim: Similar patterns of basement membrane gene expression were verified between kidney organoids and human and mouse fetal kidneys, especially for collagen IV and laminin isoforms.
source: We also verified similar patterns of BM gene expression between kidney organoids and human and mouse fetal kidneys, especially for collagen IV and laminin isoforms.
evidence: This is based on comparative scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: Kidney organoids are a highly tractable model that can be used to study the dynamic nature of human basement membrane assembly in both health and disease.
source: Thus, we conclude that kidney organoids are a highly tractable model that can be used to study the dynamic nature of human BM assembly in both health and disease.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion of the study based on all experimental findings.
